blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A non-parametric (distribution-free) test does not assume that the data come from a particular distribution such as the Normal. Most such tests replace each value by its rank or its sign. Use one when the outcome is ordinal, when a small sample is clearly non-Normal, or when a few extreme outliers would dominate a mean-based test.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The t-test and ANOVA rely on roughly Normal data (recall §9.2.4). Non-parametric tests drop that requirement by working with the order of the values rather than their size. The price is some loss of power (recall §8.4) when the data really are Normal.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Hospital length of stay is right-skewed (recall §3.9). In a small study comparing two wards, a few patients who stay for weeks would pull each ward’s mean far to the right. The Mann-Whitney U test (§10.2) sees only who ranks above whom, so a 40-day stay counts as “the longest”, no more.

points.html: Use them for ordinal outcomes (means are not meaningful, recall §2.5 and §1.1.2.2), small samples with clear non-Normality, or outliers you cannot justify removing.

Ranking makes a test resistant to outliers, because an extreme value can only take the top (or bottom) rank. It does not make the test blind to shape: for example, the Mann-Whitney test reads as a comparison of medians only when the two groups’ distributions have a similar shape (§10.2).
When the parametric assumptions hold, the non-parametric test is somewhat less powerful. When they fail badly, it can be the more powerful of the two.

The rank tests mirror Chapter 9: sign test and Wilcoxon signed-rank ↔︎ paired t-test; Mann-Whitney ↔︎ independent-samples t-test; Kruskal-Wallis ↔︎ one-way ANOVA; Friedman ↔︎ repeated-measures ANOVA. For categorical outcomes the chi-square family (§10.6), Fisher’s exact test (§10.7) and McNemar’s test (§10.8) take over.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The sign test is a test for paired data. It records only whether each pair’s difference is positive or negative and asks whether the two signs are equally likely. Under the null hypothesis (H₀, recall §8.2) that the median difference is zero, the number of positive differences among n non-zero differences follows a Binomial(n, 0.5) distribution (recall §5.7.1.2). A test of a proportion against a fixed value using this exact distribution is the exact binomial test (recall §9.1.1); the sign test applies it to the signs of paired differences.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If an intervention does nothing, each person is as likely to go up as to go down, like a coin toss. Count the rises. If there are far more (or far fewer) than half, the coin looks biased. Pairs with a difference of exactly zero carry no sign and are dropped, so n is the number of non-zero differences. The test uses only the direction of each change, so it is valid for purely ordinal scores, where “improved by two points” and “improved by one point” cannot be compared in size.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. Under H₀, each non-zero difference is positive with probability 0.5, independently of the others.
  2. So X = number of positives ~ Binomial(n, 0.5), and P(X = k) = C(n, k) × 0.5ⁿ (recall §5.7.1.2).
  3. The p-value is the probability, under H₀, of a split at least as lopsided as the one observed. Binomial(n, 0.5) is symmetric, so the two-sided p-value is twice the smaller tail (recall §8.6).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Twelve anaemic women at a PHC had their haemoglobin (Hb) measured before and after a course of iron–folic acid tablets. The changes (after − before, g/dL) were: +0.8, +0.4, +1.1, −0.3, +0.7, +0.9, +0.6, −0.2, +1.0, +1.2, +0.5, +1.3. Ten rose and two fell. The mean change is 0.67 g/dL and the median change 0.75 g/dL.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. n = 12 non-zero differences; X = 10 positives, 2 negatives.
  2. The smaller count is 2. P(X ≤ 2) = [C(12, 0) + C(12, 1) + C(12, 2)] ÷ 2¹² = (1 + 12 + 66) ÷ 4,096 = 79 ÷ 4,096 = 0.0193.
  3. Two-sided p = 2 × 0.0193 = 0.039.
  4. At the 5% level you reject H₀: the rises outnumber the falls by more than chance alone would usually give.

blocks.alt: Binomial(12, 0.5) distribution of the number of rises, with the tails at 2 or fewer and 10 or more shaded
blocks.caption: Figure 10.1. The sign test for the 12 women. If iron had no effect, the number of rises would follow Binomial(12, 0.5). The shaded tails (≤ 2 and ≥ 10) each hold probability 0.019, giving a two-sided p of 0.039.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
hb <- read.csv("data/sign_test_hb.csv")
d  <- hb$hb_after - hb$hb_before       # change in Hb, g/dL
table(sign(d))                         # -1 = fell, 1 = rose
binom.test(sum(d > 0), sum(d != 0))    # exact sign test

-1  1 
 2 10

number of successes = 10, number of trials = 12, p-value = 0.03857
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5158623 0.9791375
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.8333333

table gives the 2 falls and 10 rises. binom.test gives the two-sided p of step 3 (0.0386). It also estimates the proportion of women whose Hb rises, 10/12 = 0.83, with an exact 95% CI of 0.52 to 0.98 (recall §7.2.4).

points.html: The sign test assumes only that the pairs are independent of each other. It makes no assumption about the shape of the differences and needs only their direction.

It throws away the size of each change, so it has low power. On these same 12 women the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which also uses the sizes, gives p = 0.002 (§10.3). Use the sign test when sizes are not meaningful (ordinal scores) or cannot be trusted.

The same exact binomial calculation tests any single proportion against a fixed value when n is small (recall §5.7.2.2.4 for when the Normal approximation is adequate). It is also the exact form of McNemar’s test (§10.8, a test for paired yes/no outcomes).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 10.1

questions.prompt: In a sign test on 10 pairs, 8 differences are positive, 1 is negative and 1 is zero. What are n and X, and what is the two-sided p-value?
questions.answer: The zero difference has no sign and is dropped, so n = 9 and X = 8 positives (1 negative). Under H₀, X ~ Binomial(9, 0.5). P(X ≥ 8) = [C(9, 8) + C(9, 9)] ÷ 2⁹ = (9 + 1) ÷ 512 = 0.0195. Two-sided p = 2 × 0.0195 = 0.039.

questions.prompt: Why is the sign test valid for a 5-point pain score when a test using the sizes of the differences may not be?
questions.answer: The sign test uses only the direction of each change (better or worse), which an ordinal score does record. A test that ranks the sizes of differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank) assumes that a change of 2 points is larger than a change of 1 point wherever it occurs on the scale, which is an interval-scale assumption that ordinal pain scores do not guarantee.
